entry.title: IST Part 2
entry.summary:
IST Part 2

During IST, I had the opportunity to visit a few different religious sites.

pashupatinath temple

A large Hindu temple in Kathmandu, I was unfortunately not allowed to actually enter the temple myself as a non-Hindu. We still had a chance to walk around the complex, see many of the buildings from the outside, as well as a few different religious ceremonies.


This is part of a Hindu puja, or prayer / worship. Puja comes in many forms at different times - at home some families perform a small puja daily, visiting small temples in the community (most areas have a small and worshipping one or more deities. At temples such as this, larger pujas are performed regularly. Pashupatinath is dedicated to a manifestation of Shiva, one of the most prominent gods in Hinduism.


Pashupatinath sits along the Bagmati River through Kathmandu. If you go later in the evening or night, the lights reflect off the water in a really beautiful way. On that bridge in the right of the picture there are some dudes who hang out and try to give you tika (a spot of red powder in the center of your forehead) and then will request money. I’m still not quite sure if people consider this a sort of scam or not. I’ve received tika on many occasions since coming to Nepal and have not yet paid for it.


This photo angle is a popular one for the temple - my picture looks pretty similar to the one you’ll see on the temple’s wikipedia page.


Many a cow roaming about freely. For those unaware, cows are considered sacred in hinduism. they can basically do whatever they want here without repercussion.


monkeys, conversely, are less sacred here. They are more or less considered nuisances. I’ve been told that if you make eye contact with them, they are more likely to attack. They’re funny little guys though, and fun to watch. I have yet to be attacked by one, but have heard some unpleasant stories from other PCVs.


Pashupatinath features several of these structures for performing cremation, called ghats. Following ancient tradition, they burn bodies here and sweep the ashes into the river. I thought they may have been performing one today, but on closer inspection it was just some logs.


This photo was a bit blurry, but you can see many more of the ghats along the river here. Kathmandu sits behind in the distance.

swayambhu mahachaitya

Swayambhu is a large Buddhist Stupa at the top of a large hill in Kathmandu. Effectively a huge dome with Buddhas eyes atop, it’s a very powerful thing to witness in person. I swung by here one night during IST to meet up with TJ and his host sister. They greeted me there and gave me a tour of the area, and shared some information about the stupa and Buddhism in general.


around the stupa there are a series of metal wheels with prayers etched in the sides, commonly seen at buddhist places of worship. You are meant to spin these wheels clockwise with your right hand, as the mantras etched on them are read from left to right. I don’t know why you are supposed to use your right hand specifically.


People can be seen here spinning the prayer wheels as they walk clockwise around the stupa.


This is a few of the smaller stupas which surround the larger one. I’m still not exactly sure what the difference is, and why there are multiple of varying sizes.


A slightly wider angle photo of the scene. It was very crowded.


I didn’t get as many photos of the monkeys as I wanted - they don’t hold still long. Swayambhu is also known to many as “The Monkey Temple”

The rest of IST itself was uneventful. We flew back from Kathmandu to Pokhara on September 28th, then got stuck in Pokhara for a few days due to poor road conditions, then headed home after that.


managed to get a nice photo of the mountains on a free day. Shortly after this those clouds on the right rolled in and covered them back up. I spent the rest of the day after this walking around through Pokhara pretty aimlessly and saw some nice neighborhoods.


Pokhara actually has a pretty neat little skate park. There’s also a few decent ones in Kathmandu. Generally, skateboarding is not that big in Nepal, but popularity is steadily growing. I swung by this one to kill some time waiting to be released back to site. Right when I was done skating, I got the OK from Peace Corps to head back home to Gorkha.

That’s all for this one. As always, thanks for reading, and I hope you have a great day. Here’s one more monkey.


~ Basanta

entry.title: IST
entry.summary:
IST

I started writing this post a few weeks ago, but never quite wrapped it up until now. I’m not going to go through and rephrase everything, so pardon me if it seems a little bit disjointed.

It’s September 24th at 1:33 AM. I just spoke with TJ for a long while about the Mandelbrot Set. The Mandelbrot Set is a popular pattern from the complex plane, the plane of numbers that can be defined via two parts, a real part, and an imaginary part. when given a number comprising these parts, then plugging it into a simple function (fc(z) = z^2 + c) recursively, it will either diverge to infinity or converge towards a single limit. The graph is color coded depending on whether it diverges, and if so how long it takes to do so. It’s pretty neat, and has a lot of really cool looking fractals as you zoom in. See a video of it here.


This photo stolen from somewhere online.

This week we are at IST, or “in service training”. This is something that all Peace Corps Volunteers will be familiar with, but usually occurs earlier in service than ours has. Ours was offset slightly due to a combination of monsoon season and splitting of IST by sector (Education went last - Agriculture and Environment sectors went before us).

With a flight to Kathmandu on Friday, the other education volunteers and I headed to Pokhara on Thursday to meet up and prepare to head over. We turned in fairly early to catch our 10 AM flight the next day.

Unfortunately our 10 AM flight was secretly a 1 PM flight in disguise. I’ve been informed this kind of delay is pretty standard for the Pokhara Airport. I spent the free time chit chatting with the other volunteers and playing Chrono Trigger. Eventually we were released to board the plane. Everyone was pretty ready to get moving by this point.


This is Leo, another teacher from my district.


I thought it was cool that the plane had propeller engines.


Pokhara Airport


A view of Kathmandu as we approached. Pokhara, despite being the second largest city in Nepal, is significantly smaller than Kathmandu (600k people vs 1.5 million in Kathmandu).

It’s funny to think about how long I’ve been here now. I’ve currently been in Nepal for about 8 and a half months, which is no small chunk of time. My language has improved, I’ve made many new friends, and I feel significantly more confident in my ability to teach. It can be easy to miss these things day to day, but when you get everyone together and look back it’s nice to think about the progress you’ve made.

The first half of IST was largely sessions between the Education volunteers and the Peace Corps staff for the Education sector. Each volunteer gave a small presentation about their site and what sort of things they are doing to improve their community. These presentations ran significantly longer than intended, as everyone took the 15 minute limit for their presentation as more of a suggestion than a hard rule. It was fun though, seeing a detailed look at everyone’s sites. Everyone approaches the work from a slightly different angle. Some are more engaged in the cultural aspects, whereas others take a much more technical approach to teaching. No strategy is better or worse than any other, it’s more of a reflection of what each individual volunteer values the most.


Leo being an angel as usual. I just realized I’ve never asked anyone’s permission to put their photo in my blog. Leo, if you’re reading this, I’d like to request to put this picture in my blog. Thanks.


TJ delivering an expertly crafted presentation about his site.

During the day, IST was really just a lot of hanging out in the hotel with the other education volunteers. It doesn’t make for particularly thrilling content, to be honest. After sessions I spent a bit more time exploring Kathmandu. I’m just going to dump a bunch of photos of that here, of varying quality. Since there’s a lot to cover for IST, I’m also going to split this into two posts, and cover the rest in the next one.


I can’t lie, I’m such a sucker for these narrow shopping ways through the city. They remind me a bit of Akihabara, Tokyo, Japan, but with less technology and more fake Nike shoes.


A photo I took out the window of an indrive, which is the Nepali equivalent of uber.


On my way to Swayambhu (which you can see peeking out at the top), a Buddhist stupa that I will cover in the next blog post.


A Nepali tailor. Me and several of the other volunteers got fitted at a shop much like this one (though not this one specifically) for our teacher uniforms. I wasn’t there at the time, but apparently one of my fellow volunteers didn’t think to ask for a changing room, and just took off all his clothes right there in the shop.


A rainy day in Kathmandu.


I can’t recall the name of this place, but I like yellow Vespas and this place had really good buff sliders.


This car looked cool so my buddy wanted his picture taken in front of it. This one came out kind of blurry. Technically I should probably blur this guy’s license plate but I don’t think anyone reading my blog has any nefarious intentions in mind, and even if you do there’s a good chance you can’t read it anyway.

That’s all for this one. I should have a lot of free time this week, as Dashain has just begun, a multi-week long holiday here in Nepal. Today was our last day of school before the holiday. I’ll detail more about the rest of IST and my arduous journey home in the next one.

As always, thanks for reading. I hope you’re having a great day wherever you are.

  • Basanta

entry.title: Shaving, Skating
entry.summary:
Shaving, Skating

Compared to the US, the bathrooms in Nepal are quite different. Next to my bedroom (the window of which is featured here) is a sink, and through the door just out of frame to the left is the latrine. Most bathrooms in Nepal feature squat toilets rather than western style, and often instead of a shower head just a tap in the wall at about waist height. I won’t get far into the logistics of using the squat toilet, but you get a hang of it pretty quick, often with a hiccup or two along the way. I’ll admit the first time is a little daunting.

This morning I shaved before I headed to school. I normally shave once every week or so. Since arriving in Nepal I’ve slightly changed my shaving habits from home, and have been exploring shaving as something I’ve done for a long time but never really paid much attention to. For those reading who shave their face, I encourage you to try safety razors for a more environmentally friendly shave, and leaving the shaving cream on a bit longer before you start shaving.


You’ll note that my window is effectively the mirror for this sink. It’s always funny when I’m in my room and one of my neighbors walks up to check their appearance before heading out for the day.

Since coming to Nepal, I have been skateboarding significantly less than I do at home. I picked up a board when I first got to my permanent site, but I didn’t really think there was anywhere I could use it. There is a large municipal building just up the road from my host family’s house which I assumed was off limits - my host brother insisted otherwise. We tried it, and some of the staff came out to watch us with the skateboard. It was a big hit.

My host brother and a few of his friends. I don’t recommend skating in slides, but they handled it well.

The kids were quickly obsessed. For the next week or so every day I would get multiple knocks on my door from various neighborhood children asking to use the skateboard. some of them standing on it, some just wanted to sit on it and go down a small hill. I’d occasionally have to tell them that someone was already using it and point them in the direction of my best guess as to where the previous group had taken the thing.

This board is pretty crummy, the pavement isn’t particularly smooth, and it can be hard to find the energy to go skating after teaching all day, especially with how hot it’s been. Still, one of the 3 official goals of the Peace Corps is sharing some American culture with Nepal, and it’s nice to have a good downtime activity for the weekends when the weather is nice.

As always, thanks for reading. If the weather is nice wherever you are, try to get out today!

  • Basanta
